steps: Nitrogen in NH₃ has an available lone pair.
Boron in BF₃ can accept that pair.
The donor is base and acceptor acid.
example.answer: NH₃ is Lewis base; BF₃ is Lewis acid.

sections.mistake: Lewis acid–base theory is not limited to species donating or accepting protons.

sections.title: Coordinate bonds in Lewis reactions
sections.summary: Lewis acid–base bonding forms a shared pair originally supplied by the base.
explain: When a Lewis base donates a pair to a Lewis acid, a coordination bond forms. It is a covalent bond whose two electrons originally came from one atom. After formation, its shared-pair description is like other covalent bonds.

A Lewis structure of the reactants should show the donor lone pair, while the product shows the new bond. Nucleophiles function as Lewis bases and electrophiles as Lewis acids because they have the same pair-donation and pair-acceptance roles.
steps: Draw the donor lone pair in the reactant Lewis structure.
Draw an arrow from donor to acceptor for bond formation.
Draw the bonded product, checking electron count and overall charge.

example.q: Explain formation of NH₄⁺ from NH₃ and H⁺ using Lewis terms.
steps: NH₃ supplies the nitrogen lone pair.
H⁺ accepts the pair.
The new N–H bond forms and the overall product has +1 charge.
example.answer: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; the new bond has a shared pair from N.

sections.mistake: The coordinate-bond arrow points from donor to acceptor, not from positive ion to donor.

sections.title: Ligands and complex-ion charges
sections.summary: Ligands donate electron pairs to a central transition-metal cation.
explain: A ligand is an ion or molecule with a donor electron pair that can coordinate to a metal centre. Neutral ligands such as H₂O or NH₃ contribute zero formal charge to the overall complex, while anionic ligands such as Cl⁻ contribute their ionic charge.

The total charge on a complex is the metal oxidation state plus the sum of ligand charges. This makes it possible either to determine complex charge from its components or infer the metal oxidation state from a known complex charge.
steps: List the metal oxidation state and every ligand charge.
Multiply each ligand charge by its count.
Add charges and write the complex in brackets with its overall charge.

example.q: Find the charge on a complex containing Co³⁺ and six NH₃ ligands.
steps: Metal contributes +3.
Each ammonia ligand is neutral, so six contribute 0.
Total charge is +3 + 0.

sections.mistake: Neutral ligands do not cancel the positive charge merely because they donate electrons into bonds.

sections.title: SN1 and SN2 mechanisms
sections.summary: Primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes follow contrasting substitution pathways in the syllabus models.
explain: The SN2 model is a concerted one-step process: a nucleophile attacks from the back of the C–leaving-group bond as that bond breaks. It has one transition state and no carbocation intermediate. Backside attack gives inversion at a suitable chiral centre, and rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile].

The SN1 model has a slow ionization step producing a carbocation and leaving group, followed by nucleophile attack. It has two steps and an intermediate, with rate = k[halogenoalkane]. Primary halogenoalkanes are treated by SN2, tertiary by SN1, and secondary substrates can follow either in the guide’s scope.
steps: Classify the carbon bonded to the leaving group as primary, secondary or tertiary.
For SN2 draw simultaneous attack and bond cleavage; for SN1 draw ionization then attack.
Relate steps to rate law, intermediate presence and stereochemical consequence.

example.q: Contrast hydroxide substitution of a primary bromoalkane with a tertiary bromoalkane.
steps: Primary: one-step backside attack; both reactants participate in the rate-determining event.
Tertiary: slow C–Br ionization forms a carbocation, followed by OH⁻ attack.
Rate laws are bimolecular and unimolecular respectively.
example.answer: Primary SN2: k[RX][OH⁻]; tertiary SN1: k[RX].

sections.mistake: SN1 has a carbocation intermediate; SN2 has a transition state but no intermediate.

sections.title: Leaving groups and substitution rates
sections.summary: A weaker carbon–halogen bond generally makes leaving-group departure easier.
explain: For otherwise comparable halogenoalkanes, substitution commonly becomes faster from chloro- to bromo- to iodo- compounds. The C–I bond is weaker than C–Br, which is weaker than C–Cl, so cleavage is easier.

Explain the trend using the relevant bond strength and leaving-group ability, not only the polarity of the bond. The guide does not assess detailed solvent effects or mechanism-dependent solvent changes for this outcome.
steps: Keep the carbon skeleton and other conditions comparable.
Compare C–halogen bond strength.
Predict faster substitution when the leaving group can depart more readily.

example.q: Rank CH₃CH₂Cl, CH₃CH₂Br and CH₃CH₂I by expected substitution rate under comparable conditions.
steps: C–Cl is strongest among these bonds.
C–I is weakest and cleaves most readily.
The bromo compound is intermediate.

sections.mistake: Greater C–Cl bond polarity alone does not mean the chloro compound reacts fastest.

sections.title: Mechanisms of electrophilic addition
sections.summary: The alkene π pair initiates addition by attacking an electrophilic reagent.
explain: For hydrogen halide addition, the π electron pair attacks H while the H–X bond pair goes to X. A carbocation forms; the halide then donates a pair to the carbocation. Acid-catalysed hydration similarly involves protonation, water attack and loss of a proton to give an alcohol.

Halogen addition begins as the electron-rich double bond polarizes the halogen molecule; electrophilic attack and halide capture produce a dihalogenoalkane. Show electron pairs moving from electron-rich bonds or lone pairs toward electron-poor centres. For detailed intermediate drawings, follow the treatment specified for the course rather than inventing unsupported charges.
steps: Start the first curly arrow at the π bond toward the electrophile.
Show breaking of the relevant reagent bond and formation of the intermediate.
Complete attack by the electron-pair donor and any required deprotonation.

example.q: Describe the pair movements in adding HBr to ethene.
steps: The C=C π pair forms a bond to H; the H–Br pair moves to Br.
An ethyl carbocation and Br⁻ result in the stepwise representation.
A Br⁻ lone pair forms the second new bond at the cationic carbon.
example.answer: Ethene + HBr → bromoethane through electrophilic attack then bromide attack.

sections.mistake: Curly arrows start at electrons, never at a bare positive charge.

sections.title: Unsymmetrical addition and carbocation stability
sections.summary: The more stable possible carbocation helps explain the major addition product.
explain: An unsymmetrical alkene can form different carbocations when protonated. More alkyl substitution generally stabilizes a carbocation: tertiary is more stable than secondary, which is more stable than primary in the simple comparison used here.

The pathway through the more stable carbocation is generally favoured, producing a major product rather than necessarily an exclusive one. Predict both possible connectivities before deciding which dominates for hydrogen halide addition or acid-catalysed hydration.
steps: Draw the two possible proton-addition orientations.
Classify the resulting carbocations.
Choose the more stable intermediate and attach halide or water-derived OH at that carbon.

example.q: Predict the major product from propene with HBr.
steps: H addition to the terminal carbon leaves a secondary carbocation on the central carbon.
The alternative leaves a less stable primary carbocation.
Br⁻ attacks the more favoured secondary carbocation.

sections.mistake: Say major product, not the only possible product, unless the question establishes exclusivity.

visual.title: Unsymmetrical addition and carbocation stability
labels: Major product via more stable cation

sections.title: Electrophilic substitution of benzene
sections.summary: Benzene replaces hydrogen to regain its delocalized ring after electrophilic attack.
explain: Benzene’s π electrons attack a charged electrophile E⁺ to make a C–E bond, temporarily disrupting the ring’s delocalized system and producing a positively charged intermediate. This costs aromatic stabilization.

A proton is then removed from the carbon bearing E; the C–H electron pair restores the delocalized π system. The overall change substitutes E for H rather than adding permanently across a ring bond. Formation of the electrophile itself is not assessed for this outcome.
steps: Draw a curly arrow from ring π electron density to E⁺.
Show the positively charged intermediate with E and H attached to the attacked carbon.
Show C–H bond electrons restoring the ring as H⁺ is lost.

example.q: Explain why benzene commonly undergoes substitution rather than simple addition with an electrophile.
steps: Initial electrophilic attack temporarily breaks the fully delocalized ring arrangement.
Losing H⁺ allows the C–H bonding pair to restore delocalization.
Substitution recovers the stabilized π system, whereas simple addition would leave it disrupted.
example.answer: Substitution restores the delocalized aromatic ring.

sections.mistake: Do not leave the final substitution product as a permanently localized carbocation.
